Philipp E. Nothaft, “Medieval Europe’s Satanic Ciphers: On the Genesis of a Modern Myth,” *British Journal for the History of Mathematics* 35, no. 2 (2020): {page}, https://doi.org/10.1080/26375451.2020.1726050. **Shortened note:** Nothaft, “Satanic Ciphers,” {page}. **Bibliography:** Nothaft, C. Philipp E. “Medieval Europe’s Satanic Ciphers: On the Genesis of a Modern Myth.” *British Journal for the History of Mathematics* 35, no. 2 (2020): 107–36. https://doi.org/10.1080/26375451.2020.1726050. ## Essay use Specialist critique of modern narratives about medieval numeral reception. The author’s Oxford repository abstract identifies demonisation and general institutional bans as claims the article challenges. The source must not be cited as evidence that those claims occurred. **Claim boundary:** the abstract establishes the article’s stated argument. Individual medieval restrictions, manuscripts, Salem and the history of cipher terminology require the article’s actual evidence and independent primary collation. No local historical case is certified from the title or abstract. ## Passages and excerpts ### nothaft-2020-satanic-ciphers-q001 — Author’s abstract: the narrative under criticism - **Locator:** author’s abstract in the [Oxford University Research Archive record](https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid%3A71f4c8ca-2b6a-4393-94dc-8d81096985bc). - **Version:** institutional record for the published 2020 article; accepted manuscript is separately listed. Journal pp.107–136 identify the article, not this unpaginated abstract. - **Relation:** Paraphrased. - **Passage:** Nothaft challenges the familiar account that medieval fear of zero’s alleged diabolical character caused wide bans on Hindu-Arabic numerals. His stated inquiry concerns the modern construction of that account and its unreliable historical foundations. - **Verification:** complete indexed institutional abstract and metadata read 2026-09-08. Direct record and accepted-manuscript download returned HTTP403; the manuscript body was not read. No quotation has been admitted. - **Use boundary:** the abstract warrants correction of this house’s former description, not detailed conclusions about every medieval jurisdiction or manuscript. The [zero-reception dossier](../../../../dossiers/zero-reception.md) **consumes** this correction by distinguishing the history of a sign’s reception from the modern reception of a story about that sign. The [reference note](../../../../concepts/reference-notes/nothaft-satanic-ciphers.md) retains its independently specified source task.

St. Martin's Press, 1987. ## Essay use Direct interlocutor for zero as meta-sign and the emergence of a meta-subject within signifying systems. The record is crucial because the essay both uses and contests Rotman's constructivist/semiotic account. **Passages needed:** “Emergence of a Meta-Subject” (chapter 2, pages 27–56 in the 1987 edition); the account of zero as meta-sign; the relation among numeral, vanishing point, and imaginary money; the work's claims about origin/absence. **Claim boundary:** preserve the divergence. Rotman develops the semiotic production of a meta-subject; the essay treats the subject as the irreducible pole whose models and signs can be observed. Assimilating the two would require a further argument about their different ontological commitments. ## Passages and excerpts No passage or excerpt has yet been gathered for this source.

It contains xii preliminary pages and 225 numbered pages. The 238-page PDF counts physical leaves; main-text printed page `n` is PDF page `n + 13`. The local filename carries Z-Library provenance and is therefore locator-only. It can establish where a scene occurs for private study; it cannot certify Kaplan quotation text. WorldCat and the Harvard Mathematics course archive independently confirm the edition family, contents, ISBN, and printed pagination. ## Chicago 18 forms **Full note:** Robert Kaplan, *The Nothing That Is: A Natural History of Zero* (New York: Oxford University Press, 2000), {page}. **Shortened note:** Kaplan, *Nothing That Is*, {page}. **Bibliography:** Kaplan, Robert. *The Nothing That Is: A Natural History of Zero*. New York: Oxford University Press, 2000. Originally published London: Allen Lane / The Penguin Press, 1999. ## Essay use Kaplan is the principal narrative companion for §1. The selected locator maps the full route from positional absence through arithmetic, the `0/1`–`1/0` mediant construction, the empty set, and one-generator logic. **Passages needed:** use a purchased or library copy before promoting any Kaplan wording. Priority pages are 4–13, 36–75, 90–115, 203–215, and 216–219. **Claim boundary:** Kaplan supplies a literary history and a map of mathematical scenes. Intercultural transmission, contested priority, Indian mathematical practice, and his compressed philosophical comparisons require specialist scholarship and primary texts. His p. 73 cancellation argument is mathematically useful within ordinary field assumptions; the cultural judgement that follows on p. 74 is not licensed as neutral history. The zero–subject historical braid takes from Kaplan the changing mathematical offices of zero and the formal scenes of `0/1` and `1/0`. It does not ask this book to establish the corresponding history of the modern subject, psychoanalysis, or Gebserian integral consciousness; those are separately sourced and brought into one authorial historical argument. ## Passages and excerpts ### Passage register These source-specific fields were gathered before consolidation and remain part of this source's evidence record. #### `kaplan-1999-nothing-that-is-q001` | `kaplan-1999-nothing-that-is-q001` | `kaplan-1999-nothing-that-is` | p. 73, exact span needed | source-matched | local extraction; check print/PDF | division by zero as historical/conceptual hinge | §1 | [[Core Theorem Bridge]] | no | ## Scholarly reading and worked material ### Material metadata - **Study id:** study-kaplan-1999-nothing-that-is - **Study status:** edition-mapped-primary-verification-partial - **Citation status:** citation-ready - **Quote status:** excerpts-unverified - **Edition status:** selected-2000-oup-locator-mapped - **Movement ids:** 13-s1-p0-sign-migrates; 14-s1-p1-sunya-operational; 15-s1-p2-empty-set-generates-one; 17-s1-p4-zero-outside-math; 18-s1-p5-loan-returns - **Source ids:** kaplan-1999-nothing-that-is; colebrooke-1817-brahmagupta-bhaskara; dutta-2023-zero-divided-numbers-india; rotman-1987-signifying-nothing; nothaft-2020-satanic-ciphers; sheffer-1913-five-postulates - **Ownership:** protected-learning-surface - **Export status:** local-only > [!warning] Three authorities, kept apart > The bibliographic authority is Kaplan — The Nothing That Is (2000 OUP printing). Frank's marginalia remain byte-for-byte in [[The Nothing That Is - Robert Kaplan]]. The local PDF is the selected 2000 Oxford printing, ISBN 0-19-512842-7: printed page `n` is PDF page `n + 13`. Its Z-Library-labelled provenance makes it locator-only. No Kaplan passage is quotation-ready. Exact primary text for Brahmagupta and Bhāskara comes instead from the public-domain [Colebrooke — Brahmagupta and Bhāskara (1817)](../../brahmagupta/colebrooke-1817-brahmagupta-bhaskara/SOURCE.md). ## Why this book is load-bearing Kaplan lets §1 be read as a history of changed permissions. A blank may keep a place without counting as a number; a mark may enter arithmetic without admitting every operation; an empty set may represent zero and become a member of one; the boundary signs `0/1` and `1/0` may generate positive rationals without becoming ordinary quotients. The sequence matters because the essay's `0/1` must emerge from operations and prohibitions, not arrive already swollen with metaphysical meaning. The book is therefore the section's narrative spine, not its sole historical authority. Kaplan's Babylonian, Indian, Arabic, and European scenes identify what needs to be understood. Primary texts and specialist histories decide what can be asserted. This division is especially important at printed pp. 73–74: the algebraic cancellation argument is useful, but Kaplan's ensuing cultural explanation of Indian mathematics is not neutral history. Read it against [Dutta — Zero-Divided Numbers in Indian Mathematics (2023)](../../dutta/dutta-2023-zero-divided-numbers-india/SOURCE.md) and the primary verses rather than inheriting its judgement. ## Historical reading spine ### 1. A place is made visible — printed pp. 4–13 Kaplan begins with Sumerian and Babylonian inscription because positional notation creates an absence that matters. In a sexagesimal number, a missing power changes every following value. Old Babylonian practice could leave the magnitude to context; later scribal practice introduced an internal separator for an absent place. The decisive operation is not “nothing becomes a number.” It is that the place where nothing is entered becomes legible enough for the surrounding marks to keep their positions. Keep the prohibition in view: Kaplan's separator is internal, not a terminal digit, and the order of magnitude can remain ambiguous. A blank, a placeholder, and zero as an arithmetic object are different historical achievements. This is the scene for [[13-s1-p0-sign-migrates]], while specialist cuneiform scholarship must carry dates, tablet identities, and priority claims. ### 2. A sign marks absent measure — printed pp. 14–27 The Greek chapter is not simply a story of lack. Greek mathematics accomplished immense constructions without positional zero, while Hellenistic astronomical notation later used a circular mark inside sexagesimal measurements. In Ptolemaic astronomy the mark can hold an absent degree, minute, or second. It behaves more like punctuation within measurement than a freely operating number. Kaplan rehearses several possible origins for the sign. Treat those as conjectures. The lesson is firmer and smaller: the same visible form can occupy a different mathematical office. A circle in an astronomical table does not yet carry the operations later assigned to zero. ### 3. Empty place enters arithmetic — printed pp. 36–75 Kaplan's eastward sequence should be learned in four stages rather than compressed into “India invented zero.” Aryabhata uses *kha* for a place within a positional procedure. Varāhamihira's vocabulary includes *kha*, *ambara*, *ākāśa*, and *śūnya*. Brahmagupta places zero among positive and negative quantities and states rules for addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, powers, and roots. Mahāvīra and Bhāskara continue the operational problem, especially where a zero denominator is retained rather than immediately evaluated. The Gwalior inscription supplies Kaplan's visible hollow-circle scene; the dust-board and dot stories supply hypotheses about how marks might arise materially. Neither settles a unique origin. The Bakhshali manuscript dating in this 2000 book is now a historical state of scholarship, not a current conclusion. At printed pp. 68–75, zero becomes more than a kept place because rules specify what happens when it meets another quantity. Three operations must stay distinct: - additive identity: adding zero leaves the other quantity unchanged; - multiplicative absorption: multiplying by zero yields zero; - zero denominator: a written expression is retained under a special rule, where ordinary cancellation cannot be assumed. The first two have a primary-text support card at `colebrooke-1817-brahmagupta-bhaskara-q001`. The third has a primary-text boundary card at `colebrooke-1817-brahmagupta-bhaskara-q002`. Bhāskara's theological comparison is not Kaplan's invention: it appears in the selected primary translation at `colebrooke-1817-brahmagupta-bhaskara-q003`. Read the mathematical invariance and the divine image together, but do not let either certify the other. ### 4. A notation crosses institutions — printed pp. 90–115 Kaplan follows Indian numerical practice through Baghdad, al-Khwārizmī, Arabic *ṣifr*, Latin adaptations, Gerbert, Fibonacci, mnemonic verse, merchants, and bookkeeping. The useful historical picture is cumulative. A notation is transmitted through texts, teaching, trade, tables, and institutions; it is renamed and repurposed as it moves. Fibonacci's *Liber Abaci* belongs to that reception history, not to a single heroic invention of European zero. The resistance matters. Written algorithms competed with counting boards; unfamiliar figures were difficult to teach and easy to alter; legal and commercial settings could treat them as fraud risks. Those conditions explain why a mathematically useful sign can remain socially unstable. Kaplan's claims about a 1299 Florentine ban, exact trader routes, and manuscript priority still require specialist verification before public prose. ### 5. Zero and one become generators — printed pp. 203–215 Chapter Fifteen is the missed centre of Frank's `0/1` inquiry. Kaplan first places `0/1` and `1/0` at the two boundaries of a rational-number construction. Repeatedly insert the mediant `(a+c)/(b+d)` between neighbours `a/b` and `c/d`; `1/1` appears between the boundaries, then `1/2` and `2/1`, and the positive rationals ramify between them. Here `1/0` is a formal boundary marker, not a licensed quotient in the ordinary field. Kaplan then changes constructions. The empty product takes value one; the empty set represents zero; von Neumann's finite-set construction lets one contain zero as a member; Peirce's down-arrow operation generates Boolean functions from repeated “neither A nor B.” These are not variations of one proof. They are four different generative procedures, and the source keeps them separate so the essay can compare them honestly. ## Read the book through five questions ### 1. How does an empty place become an operative sign? Read printed pp. 4–13, 14–27, and 36–56 in sequence. On each pass identify the material mark, the problem it solves, and what it still cannot do. The Babylonian separator stabilises an internal place; the astronomical circle holds an absent measure; the Indian sign and vocabulary enter positional and then arithmetic practice. Return to [[13-s1-p0-sign-migrates]] able to state the change without calling all three objects “zero” in the same sense. ### 2. What changes when *śūnya* enters arithmetic? Read Kaplan's printed pp. 68–75 beside [Colebrooke passages](../../brahmagupta/colebrooke-1817-brahmagupta-bhaskara/SOURCE.md#passages). Work through addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division one operation at a time. The primary verses prevent the history from becoming Kaplan's paraphrase; Kaplan supplies the narrative transition by which rules change the sign's status. The consumer is [[14-s1-p1-sunya-operational]]. A statement about Indian “nothingness” earns no place here unless it names a text, an operation, and a boundary. The section's stronger point is that arithmetic citizenship is distributed unevenly: zero can be an additive identity and multiplicative absorber while division remains a contested edge. ### 3. Which law fails at a zero denominator? Kaplan's printed p. 73 uses `6·0 = 17·0` and shows that cancelling the common zero would identify 6 and 17. Printed p. 74 correctly returns ordinary arithmetic to the prohibition, then moves into an explanation of why Indian mathematicians supposedly failed to make that move. Keep the proof and reject the cultural inference as a warrant. Dutta reconstructs another possibility: retain zero-denominator expressions while forbidding cancellation or cross-multiplication in that regime, and sometimes postpone evaluation. This does not make `a/0` an ordinary field quotient. It shows why the container must be named before an expression is judged. That distinction belongs to [[17-s1-p4-zero-outside-math]]. ### 4. In what exact sense does one contain zero? At printed pp. 208–212, separate the empty product from the von Neumann construction. The empty product equals one because one is the multiplicative identity. The set construction begins with `0 = ∅` and defines each successor by adjoining the preceding set. In that representation, `1 = {0}`, so `0 ∈ 1`. “Contains” means membership in this construction. It does not mean that one and zero are identical, that every definition of natural number must use these sets, or that the empty set is awareness. This is the licensed formal floor for [[15-s1-p2-empty-set-generates-one]]. ### 5. What does one logical generator actually generate? Kaplan's printed pp. 212–215 teach the Peirce down-arrow as NOR: `p ↓ q = ¬(p ∨ q)`, “neither p nor q.” He then connects the result to Sheffer and Wittgenstein. The formal sequence can be checked: NOR generates negation by `p ↓ p`, and disjunction by denying the denied result. Kaplan's historical and philosophical transitions remain secondary claims needing Peirce, Sheffer, and Wittgenstein in their own texts. Modern NAND is also functionally complete, but it is a different connective: `p | q = ¬(p ∧ q)`. The existing NAND exercise remains below as a comparison. It must not be reported as Kaplan's operation or silently attributed to Sheffer's 1913 notation. [Sheffer — A Set of Five Independent Postulates (1913)](../../sheffer/sheffer-1913-five-postulates/SOURCE.md) is citation-ready but its exact movement remains unassigned. The QL slash has its own derivation; functional completeness can become a defined resonance only after that difference is stated. ## Mathematical workbench ### Division by zero: run the ordinary-field collapse Suppose `z` were an ordinary multiplicative inverse of zero, so `0z = 1`. For any field element `a`, \[ a=a\cdot1=a(0z)=(a0)z=0z=1. \] Every element would equal one: ordinary field laws collapse every number when zero is given an inverse without any other change. This proof uses multiplicative identity, the proposed inverse, associativity, and zero absorption. Kaplan's printed p. 73 gives a concrete cancellation version; it is related, not identical. A non-collapsing extension must restrict or reinterpret at least one of those moves. **Try it:** mark the exact step Dutta's zero-divided regime refuses. Then state whether the refusal concerns multiplication, cancellation, cross-multiplication, or equality. “Division by zero works differently” is too loose to count as an answer. **Check your work:** the decisive refusal is the inference from equal zero-products to equal factors, or its fraction-form equivalent. Ordinary fields already forbid cancellation by zero. A system can retain a written zero-denominator object only by specifying further laws rather than inheriting all field laws unchanged. ### `0/1` and `1/0`: build the rational interval Begin with Kaplan's two formal boundary fractions: \[ \frac01,\qquad \frac10. \] Between neighbours `a/b` and `c/d`, insert their mediant `(a+c)/(b+d)`. The first three rows are: \[ \frac01,\ \frac11,\ \frac10, \] \[ \frac01,\ \frac12,\ \frac11,\ \frac21,\ \frac10, \] \[ \frac01,\ \frac13,\ \frac12,\ \frac23,\ \frac11,\ \frac32,\ \frac21,\ \frac31,\ \frac10. \] The operation makes the essay's boundary pair mathematically active: neither endpoint is consumed, yet relations proliferate between them. Do not call `1/0` infinity here without declaring a chosen extended structure. In this construction it is a goalpost that lets the mediant operation reach every positive scale. **Try it:** locate `3/5`. Start between `0/1` and `1/1`, then follow the mediants until it appears. Record the left and right parents whose numerators and denominators add to 3 and 5. **Check your work:** `3/5` appears between `1/2` and `2/3`, since `(1+2)/(2+3)=3/5`. Kaplan calls the wider construction a Farey sequence; the precise relation to Farey sequences and the Stern–Brocot tree remains a specialist verification target. ### Von Neumann ordinals: build three numbers from the empty set Start with `0 = ∅` and define `S(n) = n ∪ {n}`: \[ 1=\{\varnothing\},\qquad 2=\{\varnothing,\{\varnothing\}\}, \] \[ 3=\{\varnothing,\{\varnothing\},\{\varnothing,\{\varnothing\}\}\}. \] Each finite ordinal is the set of its predecessors. Zero is a member of every non-zero finite ordinal in this representation. The operative fact is successive inclusion, not a slogan in which “nothing creates everything.” **Try it:** write `S(3)` using only the preceding sets, then point to the new singleton. **Check your work:** `S(3)=3∪{3}={0,1,2,3}`. Kaplan gives the nested construction at printed p. 211; the explicit successor equation belongs to standard set-theoretic teaching and should be sourced independently in public prose. ### Kaplan's NOR route Let `p ↓ q = ¬(p ∨ q)`. Its truth table is true only when both inputs are false. Repetition reconstructs negation and disjunction: \[ \neg p=p\downarrow p, \] \[ p\lor q=(p\downarrow q)\downarrow(p\downarrow q). \] Conjunction then follows by De Morgan's law: \[ p\land q=(p\downarrow p)\downarrow(q\downarrow q). \] This is the one-generator result Kaplan teaches at printed pp. 212–215. Its historical naming and attribution must be checked against the primary Peirce, Sheffer, and *Tractatus* passages before it becomes citation prose. ### Modern NAND workbench For comparison, let `p | q = ¬(p ∧ q)`. Negation and conjunction become: \[ \neg p=p\mid p, \] \[ p\land q=(p\mid q)\mid(p\mid q). \] **Try it:** derive `p ∨ q` using only `|`. **Check your work:** `p∨q=(p|p)|(q|q)`. The exercise establishes modern NAND functional completeness. It does not reproduce Kaplan's NOR route, determine Sheffer's historical notation, or supply the QL slash with a metaphysical meaning. ## Passage and provenance ledger No Kaplan passage is quotation-ready. The selected local printing fixes these locator maps without authorising copied text: | Printed locator | PDF locator | What is actually there | Licensed use now | |---|---:|---|---| | pp. 4–13 | pp. 17–26 | Sumerian/Babylonian positional notation and the internal separator | taught historical scene; dates and tablets need specialist sources | | pp. 14–27 | pp. 27–40 | Greek non-positional systems and astronomical zero mark | taught distinction; sign-origin hypotheses remain conjectural | | pp. 36–75 | pp. 49–88 | Indian signs, terms, inscription, and arithmetic rules | narrative map paired with Colebrooke primary text | | pp. 73–74 | pp. 86–87 | Bhāskara, *khahara*, cancellation collapse, then a cultural judgement | mathematical lead; cultural explanation explicitly contested | | p. 169 | p. 182 | Euler, extrema, and zero derivatives | corrects Frank's earlier late-chapter grouping | | pp. 173–174 | pp. 186–187 | Robinson's non-standard analysis and Morgenstern's removed-space image | infinitesimal/procedure lead; not Bernoulli material | | pp. 203–215 | pp. 216–228 | binary, mediants, Salem Codex, empty product, empty set, von Neumann, NOR, Wittgenstein | four separate workbenches; Salem and historical claims remain debts | | pp. 216–219 | pp. 229–232 | vacuous truth, non-being, language, Nāgārjuna, Kant, self | literary closing junction; compressed comparative claims need primary sources | The 225-versus-240-page catalogue difference is a counting convention within the same edition family, not evidence that the printed locators shift. The local object has xii preliminary pages and 225 numbered pages; the PDF has 238 physical pages. ## Return to the essay After reading, return with a scene rather than a summary: 1. name the sign or written object; 2. state the operation it permits; 3. state the operation it still forbids; 4. give Kaplan's printed locator and the quote status; 5. name the primary or specialist authority required; 6. name one movement consumer. Use the full command form from the project root, for example: ```bash python3 tools/okf-workspace.py --project-root . context 14-s1-p1-sunya-operational --depth 2 --json python3 tools/okf-workspace.py --project-root . open kaplan-1999-nothing-that-is --json python3 tools/okf-workspace.py --project-root . open colebrooke-1817-brahmagupta-bhaskara --json python3 tools/okf-workspace.py --project-root . open colebrooke-1817-brahmagupta-bhaskara-q001 --json ``` Ask the agent for one historical scene, one primary rule, one exercise, and one boundary relevant to the paragraph under composition. If the answer merges Kaplan's narrative, Colebrooke's primary wording, and the source's mathematical teaching into one authority, stop and reopen the three objects separately. ### Acquisition card - **Kaplan quotation:** inspect a purchased or library copy of ISBN 0-19-512842-7 before creating a quotation-ready Kaplan passage card. The local copy remains locator-only. - **Historical control:** acquire cuneiform tablet scholarship, a critical *Almagest*, critical Brahmagupta/Bhāskara editions, al-Khwārizmī transmission scholarship, and a primary *Liber Abaci* carrier. - **Formal control:** verify the mediant construction against Stern–Brocot/Farey scholarship; acquire von Neumann 1923; verify Peirce 1880, Sheffer 1913, and *Tractatus* 5.101, 5.5, and 6.001 separately. - **Comparative control:** Kaplan's printed pp. 216–219 compress Parmenides, *brahman*, *śūnyatā*, Nāgārjuna, Kant, and Wittgenstein.
